title: CASE OF KALUCZA v. HUNGARY
conclusion: Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Positive obligations)
summary: In the case of Kalucza v. Hungary, the applicant, Ms. Kalucza, a woman of Roma origin living in Budapest, brought a complaint against the Hungarian state. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma and Traveller women facing domestic violence, and the difficulties they encounter in obtaining effective protection from the authorities. Between 2005 and 2010, Ms. Kalucza endured repeated physical assaults and threats from her partner, Gy.B., with whom she shared an apartment. Despite numerous criminal complaints, medical reports documenting her injuries, and repeated requests for restraining orders, the Hungarian authorities failed to provide her with adequate protection. The courts often dismissed her requests for restraining orders, citing mutual animosity or lack of evidence, and criminal proceedings were frequently delayed or discontinued. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees the right to respect for private and family life. The Court found that Hungary had violated its positive obligations under Article 8 by failing to protect Ms. Kalucza from domestic violence and to provide an effective legal framework for her protection. This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it underscores the need for states to address the intersectional vulnerabilities faced by Roma women, who have historically been at heightened risk of violence and institutional neglect in Europe.
